notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: CORRECTED. Wainwright joined Doubleday at about 10.30 a. m. and moved the three batteries with him across the fields toward the seminary. The Third Division reached the field toward 11 (Rowley): Biddle's brigade about 11 a. m., formed on the extreme left a third of a mile in front of the seminary facing west (the 151st Pennsylvania, 10.30 a. m.); Stone posted his brigade at 11 a. m. between the two brigades of Wadsworth's division, right on the Chambersburg road and left nearly to the wood held by Meredith; the 150th Pennsylvania gives about noon. Robinson's division was placed in reserve near the seminary and the First Brigade (Paul) set to intrench the ridge; Baxter reached the front at 11 a. m. Doubleday directed Robinson to the seminary, sent Stone to the open space on the right of the wood and Biddle to the left and rear of the Iron Brigade toward the Millerstown road, Rowley having charge of that part of the line. CORRECTED: Rowley did not take command of the division on Jul 1: his report says the command had devolved on him the day previous (Jun 30). NOT documented: the hour at which each battery of the Artillery Brigade came up. Remains unsupported: the arrival hour of each battery of the Artillery Brigade.
notes_before: Arrival of Wainwright and Robinson at the Seminary is primary-supported (Wainwright about 10.30 a.m., earlier than the row's window start; Stone about 12 m. per audit, OCR '13 m.'). Rowley report (R055 p.313) confirms Stone and Wister were disabled and Dana took the Second Brigade; 'Rowley takes command' as a dated change not verified. Biddle toward Millerstown Rd not checked.

Pettigrew's brigade moved down the pike early on the morning of Jul 1, deployed about 2.5 miles from the town, crossed to the right of the pike (other regiments having been engaged for some time), took position behind the batteries for about half an hour, advanced half a mile to a skirt of woods and stood in line of battle until orders to advance came at 2 p. m., with Brockenbrough's brigade on its left. notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: CORRECTED. Howard received orders at 3.30 a. m. to bring the Eleventh Corps within supporting distance and at 8 a. m. the order to march to Gettysburg; Schurz's Third Division left camp at 7 a. m. by Horner's Mills. Dilger's battery arrived at about 10 a. m. (Osborn: a little after 10), Bancroft's battery at 11 a. m., the 45th New York at 11 a. m., Schurz himself about 11.30. Howard places the head of the corps "about this time" after 12.30 p. m.; the First Division came by the Emmitsburg road proper (the 75th Ohio about 1 p. m., the 17th Connecticut between 1 and 2); Steinwehr reached the field at about 2 o'clock; Schurz had the first two divisions deployed about 2 p. m. NOT documented: Howard's expectation of the corps "a little after one"; the Baltimore pike as a route (the Third Division's own report prints a blank for its hour of arrival). The hour of the "head" is carried as scenarios. Remains unsupported: Howard's expectation of the corps "a little after one" and any Baltimore pike route; the hour at which the Third Division itself entered the town (blank in Schurz's report).

corrected_claim_text: Howard received orders at 3.30 a. m. to bring the Eleventh Corps within supporting distance and at 8 a. m. the order to march to Gettysburg; Schurz's Third Division left camp at 7 a. m. by Horner's Mills. Dilger's battery arrived at about 10 a. m. (Osborn: a little after 10), Bancroft's battery at 11 a. m., the 45th New York at 11 a. m., Schurz himself about 11.30. Howard places the head of the corps "about this time" after 12.30 p. m.; the First Division came by the Emmitsburg road proper (the 75th Ohio about 1 p. m., the 17th Connecticut between 1 and 2); Steinwehr reached the field at about 2 o'clock; Schurz had the first two divisions deployed about 2 p. m. NOT documented: Howard's expectation of the corps "a little after one"; the Baltimore pike as a route (the Third Division's own report prints a blank for its hour of arrival). The hour of the "head" is carried as scenarios.

notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: CORRECTED. Baxter reached the front where the battle was raging at 11 a. m.; two regiments (the 11th Pennsylvania and 97th New York) went to the front, the other four were ordered forward in a very few moments and formed on their right, on the right of the First Division (Wadsworth), a division of the Eleventh Corps being at least 400 yards to the right; Coulter: the firing became general about 12.30 p. m.; the line held until after 3 p. m., when the brigade, out of ammunition, was relieved by part of the First (Paul's) Brigade; Baxter was engaged over two hours. Doubleday: Baxter formed on the right of Wadsworth's division, an interval of nearly 400 yards remaining to the Eleventh Corps; finding Baxter in danger of being overpowered he sent Robinson with Paul's brigade, part posted as a support to Baxter and part perpendicular to the line to protect the right flank. notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: CORRECTED. Early, on arriving in sight of Gettysburg on the Heidlersburg road, found Rodes' division engaged with the enemy to the right of him and "immediately ordered my troops to the front" and formed his line across the Heidlersburg road, with Gordon on the right, Hoke's brigade (under Colonel Avery) on the left, Hays in the centre, Smith's in rear of Hoke's; Jones' battalion of artillery was posted on the left of the road in front of Hoke and opened on the enemy's infantry and artillery. notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED. No report of Rodes' division gives one hour for its attack. Confederate regimental reports date the engagement from about noon (26th Alabama: engaged the enemy about 12 m.; 2nd North Carolina Battalion between 12 m. and 1 p. m.; the 53rd North Carolina in line about 1 o'clock). Doubleday (Union clock) has Ewell's forces advancing about 1.30 p. m. in two deployed lines supported by a third; Lee, Hill and Howard date the arrival of Rodes' or Ewell's force on the field at 2.30 (Howard 2.45 for the enemy in force in front of the Eleventh Corps); Davis about 3; the Battles and Leaders article has Rodes give the order to attack at 2.30 p. m. and a Pennsylvania regiment dates Iverson's advance about 2.30; the National Park Service CLR has the four brigades advance beginning around 2:30. The row's "uncoordinated" attack is Rodes' and Ewell's own account of the Alabama brigade (confusion, direction different from orders). All hours are carried as scenarios; the delegated default is 14:00 inside the window 13:30-14:30 and is not changed here. Remains unsupported: one hour for the attack of Rodes' division (the reports differ from about 12:00 to about 15:00); a Rodes clock: neither Rodes nor Iverson nor O'Neal gives an hour.
notes_before: Only Doubleday gives a clock (about 13:30, for Ewell's forces). Rodes, Iverson, O'Neal, Daniel, Ramseur give none. The spread 13:30 (Doubleday; NPS-Sem) / 14:00 (W-FD) / 14:30 (SS) is carried as a range; non-OR values are secondary. The Union/Confederate clock-offset remark is an inference no source states. notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: CORRECTED. Iverson and Rodes both say the Union troops fired from behind a stone wall: Iverson found the enemy "strongly posted in woods and behind a concealed stone wall", Rodes that Iverson suffered "from the enemy's musketry fire from behind a stone wall along the crest of the ridge". The 88th Pennsylvania (Baxter's brigade) was drawn up in line of battle along a stone fence; the 97th New York's skirmishers drew fire from a stone wall and the embankment of the road; the 104th New York (Paul's brigade) later drove the enemy from a stone wall covered with thick underbrush and took position behind it. The National Park Service says a stone fence ran along the eastern boundary of the Forney farm on Oak Ridge, that troops used stone fences such as those along Oak Ridge as breastworks and that Baxter's and Paul's brigades lay in part behind overgrown and tumbled-down stone walls there (secondary); Battles and Leaders puts Paul's brigade behind the stone walls of a field facing west and Baxter's facing north. No report says the wall was built during the battle: a pre-existing wall is the inference; no construction animation. The reports do not name Baxter's brigade at "the" wall by that name for the whole line. Remains unsupported: an 1863 source that says the wall pre-existed (the National Park Service says so; no report of the battle says when it was built); which regiments of Baxter's brigade lay at the wall by name beyond the 88th Pennsylvania.
notes_before: The OR confirms a stone wall in front of Iverson on the Union crest; it does not name Baxter's brigade at it (Baxter's report mentions no wall) and nowhere says it was built during the battle. Pre-existing wall is an inference; the no-construction-animation treatment stands.

notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: CORRECTED. Blackford (July 17): "The corps was deployed 2 miles from Gettysburg, with the left resting upon the Heidlersburg pike", moved forward "driving in the cavalry vedettes", met "a large force of cavalry ... in line, with a heavy line of men dismounted as skirmishers": "The former charged us twice, but were easily repulsed. After an hour or more of active skirmishing, the enemy's infantry advanced in force through the town". Against the centre "no movement by any force heavier than a double line of sharpshooters, whom our men invariably drove back, charging them once in gallant style"; on the extreme left the enemy "advanced in three lines" and the men "retired, firing from tree to tree until they met Gordon's brigade advancing, after which they were rallied on the center at the sound of my bugle". Rodes: "the sharpshooters of the Alabama brigade, under that promising young officer, Major [Eugene] Blackford, of the Fifth Alabama"; O'Neal: "Major Blackford, commanding corps of sharpshooters". Union side: Devin's cavalry brigade was driven back "by the advance of the enemy's line of battle, coming from the direction of Heidlersburg" and held "the rebel line in check for two hours, until relieved by the arrival of the Eleventh Corps"; the 45th New York's skirmish line "encountered a battalion of Alabama sharpshooters, under Major Blackford, stretched along the lane at the foot of Oak Hill". No source names the Union cavalry that Blackford met (the identification with Devin's brigade is not made by either report) and none gives an hour for the skirmish, the repulse or the rally; the window opens at 12:00 with the first Confederate hours for the division and ends at the evening edge; the sharpshooters were ahead of the division, so the first contact may be earlier. No clock offset between Union and Confederate reports is applied. Remains unsupported: the hour of the cavalry repulse, the skirmish and the rally (no report gives one).
notes_before: Both quotes verified. Arms (cavalry) not named; hour not stated, as the row says.

corrected_claim_text: Blackford (July 17): "The corps was deployed 2 miles from Gettysburg, with the left resting upon the Heidlersburg pike", moved forward "driving in the cavalry vedettes", met "a large force of cavalry ... in line, with a heavy line of men dismounted as skirmishers": "The former charged us twice, but were easily repulsed. After an hour or more of active skirmishing, the enemy's infantry advanced in force through the town". Against the centre "no movement by any force heavier than a double line of sharpshooters, whom our men invariably drove back, charging them once in gallant style"; on the extreme left the enemy "advanced in three lines" and the men "retired, firing from tree to tree until they met Gordon's brigade advancing, after which they were rallied on the center at the sound of my bugle". Rodes: "the sharpshooters of the Alabama brigade, under that promising young officer, Major [Eugene] Blackford, of the Fifth Alabama"; O'Neal: "Major Blackford, commanding corps of sharpshooters". Union side: Devin's cavalry brigade was driven back "by the advance of the enemy's line of battle, coming from the direction of Heidlersburg" and held "the rebel line in check for two hours, until relieved by the arrival of the Eleventh Corps"; the 45th New York's skirmish line "encountered a battalion of Alabama sharpshooters, under Major Blackford, stretched along the lane at the foot of Oak Hill". No source names the Union cavalry that Blackford met (the identification with Devin's brigade is not made by either report) and none gives an hour for the skirmish, the repulse or the rally; the window opens at 12:00 with the first Confederate hours for the division and ends at the evening edge; the sharpshooters were ahead of the division, so the first contact may be earlier. No clock offset between Union and Confederate reports is applied.

time_window.text: Jul 1, from about 12:00 into the afternoon; the report gives no hour (the infantry advance through the town came after an hour or more of skirmishing; Gordon's brigade was ordered forward a little after 2 o'clock, Hays)
time_window.basis: Blackford OR27-2-R527 pp.597-598; Rodes R506 p.557; O'Neal R523 p.594; Daniel R507 p.566; Hays R472 p.479; Devin OR27-1-R339 p.939; 45th New York sketch, New York at Gettysburg vol.1 p.378. Window limits: the start 12:00 is the hour at which Rodes' division, marching with the sharpshooters ahead of it, was about 2.5 miles from the town (about 12 m., Daniel R507 p.566); Blackford's corps was deployed 2 miles out; no report dates its first contact; the end 18:00 is the start of evening (tolerances.json time.day_parts). A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED. Hill: "About 2.30 o'clock, the right wing of Ewell's corps made its appearance on my left ... Pender's division was then ordered forward, Thomas' brigade being retained in reserve". Perrin: the brigade "remained in this position until about 3 o'clock, and were again ordered forward", then "probably until after 4 o'clock, when I was ordered by General Pender to advance, and to pass General Heth's division should I come up with it at a halt", and he "passed Brigadier-General Pettigrew's brigade, the men of which seemed much exhausted"; he found himself without support, Scales halted near the fence and Lane's brigade not in sight, and estimates the enemy artillery on the left "at least thirty pieces". Scales: advanced "after the lapse of some thirty minutes" under "severe artillery fire", "Every discharge made sad havoc", "Every field officer of the brigade save one had been disabled", he was wounded by a shell. Lane: deployed the Seventh North Carolina "to protect our flank, which was exposed to the enemy's cavalry", met cavalry and a few infantry from the woods and was ordered not to advance farther. Gamble: dismounted cavalry behind a stone wall opened "a sharp and rapid carbine fire" and fell back when overwhelmed. Thomas: moved to within about a mile in support of Heth's division and "remained until near sunset". Wainwright: twelve guns concentrated "hardly 5 yards apart" and Stewart's battery enfilading the line along the pike. The gun count: Wainwright has twelve guns concentrated beside Stewart's battery, Hunt (chief of artillery) sixteen guns concentrated (L 1st New York, 5th Maine, B 1st Pennsylvania) with Stewart's six 12-pounders on the same line (22 in all), Perrin an estimate of at least thirty pieces; the seed's "about 20 guns of Wainwright" devastating Scales lies among these and no report names Scales with a number of guns. NOT in any report or library text read: "a 50-yard gap between the 121st PA and Gamble's cavalry". The hours differ between orders and movements and are carried as scenarios; no clock offset is applied. Remains unsupported: a source linking a number of guns (about 20) to the devastation of Scales' brigade (the counts are 12 to 22 and unlinked); the 50-yard gap between the 121st Pennsylvania and Gamble's cavalry (no source); one hour for the advance of Pender's division (the reports give 14:30 for the order, about 15:00 and after 16:00 for the movements).
notes_before: Re-read: Hill's order follows Ewell's 2.30 appearance; Perrin's own movement is after 4 p.m. Row's 16:00 matches Perrin/W-FD; 14:30 (Hill order) and 15:30 (NPS-Sem) may be order vs advance hours. The 50-yard gap with the 121st PA, Scales's devastation and Lane's delay are not verified here.

corrected_claim_text: Hill: "About 2.30 o'clock, the right wing of Ewell's corps made its appearance on my left ... Pender's division was then ordered forward, Thomas' brigade being retained in reserve". Perrin: the brigade "remained in this position until about 3 o'clock, and were again ordered forward", then "probably until after 4 o'clock, when I was ordered by General Pender to advance, and to pass General Heth's division should I come up with it at a halt", and he "passed Brigadier-General Pettigrew's brigade, the men of which seemed much exhausted"; he found himself without support, Scales halted near the fence and Lane's brigade not in sight, and estimates the enemy artillery on the left "at least thirty pieces". Scales: advanced "after the lapse of some thirty minutes" under "severe artillery fire", "Every discharge made sad havoc", "Every field officer of the brigade save one had been disabled", he was wounded by a shell. Lane: deployed the Seventh North Carolina "to protect our flank, which was exposed to the enemy's cavalry", met cavalry and a few infantry from the woods and was ordered not to advance farther. Gamble: dismounted cavalry behind a stone wall opened "a sharp and rapid carbine fire" and fell back when overwhelmed. Thomas: moved to within about a mile in support of Heth's division and "remained until near sunset". Wainwright: twelve guns concentrated "hardly 5 yards apart" and Stewart's battery enfilading the line along the pike. The gun count: Wainwright has twelve guns concentrated beside Stewart's battery, Hunt (chief of artillery) sixteen guns concentrated (L 1st New York, 5th Maine, B 1st Pennsylvania) with Stewart's six 12-pounders on the same line (22 in all), Perrin an estimate of at least thirty pieces; the seed's "about 20 guns of Wainwright" devastating Scales lies among these and no report names Scales with a number of guns. NOT in any report or library text read: "a 50-yard gap between the 121st PA and Gamble's cavalry". The hours differ between orders and movements and are carried as scenarios; no clock offset is applied.

corrected_claim_text: Howard (10 p. m., Jul 1): "The loss in my corps is about 3,000 killed, wounded, and missing. In the two corps we have lost one piece of artillery". Howard (report): at 3.20 p. m. the enemy renewed his attack, Schurz, "engaged with a force of the enemy much larger than his own", asked for a brigade and Coster's brigade was pushed out "to cover the retreat"; at 4.10 "the troops were already giving way"; the movement was executed "with considerable confusion, on account of the First and Eleventh Corps coming together in the town"; at 4.30 "the columns reached Cemetery Hill"; "In passing through the town we lost many prisoners". Schurz: the retreat through the town was effected with the streets "filled with vehicles of every description and overrun with men of the First Corps"; "A considerable number of men ... were taken prisoners"; "It was after 5 o'clock when the Eleventh Corps occupied the position on Cemetery Hill"; "By the losses sustained in the battle of July 1, the Third Division was reduced to an effective force of about 1,500 men". Ewell: Early's and Rodes' divisions together "captured over 4,000 prisoners and three pieces of artillery"; Hill: "for the Third Corps, 2 pieces of artillery and 2,300 prisoners" (the Union corps are not distinguished). NOT in any report read: the seed's about 3,200 lost and about 1,400 prisoners for the Eleventh Corps (Wikipedia); the casualty return of the corps is a three-day figure (3,801 in a Pennsylvania volume) and the return table is unreadable in the OCR. The Jul 1 loss is therefore carried as a range from about 3,000 (Howard) to not more than the three-day total.

A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

Doubleday: "When all the troops at this point were overpowered, Captain Glenn, of the One hundred and forty-ninth Pennsylvania Volunteers, in command of my headquarters guard, defended the building for fully twenty minutes against a whole brigade of the enemy, enabling the few remaining troops, the ambulances, artillery, &c., to retreat in comparative safety"; he himself "remained at the seminary superintending the final movement" until hostile bayonets appeared around the building. The regimental account of the 149th Pennsylvania (1914 volume): "Company D, of the One hundred and forty-ninth Regiment, under Captain Glenn, which had been acting as headquarter guard, was ordered to deploy near the Fairfield road, which they did, and opened a fire sufficient to induce the enemy to halt, supposing that our forces had made a stand there. At the same time they assisted some of the artillerymen to put one of Reynold's guns in position, from which three shots were fired. This action delayed the rebels about twenty minutes and enabled the artillerymen to take off all the guns except one, which was spiked and left." The two accounts agree on a stand of about twenty minutes and differ on place and manner (the building against a brigade; a line near the Fairfield road beside a gun). Neither gives an hour: the seed's 16:00-16:20 is not in either; the window is bounded by Wadsworth's 3.45 and Howard's 4.30. No clock offset is applied. Remains unsupported: an hour for Glenn's stand (no source gives one; the seed 16:00-16:20 is not in Doubleday or the 149th Pennsylvania).
notes_before: Verified with context (Capt. Glenn, 149th PA, headquarters guard). The 16:00-16:20 clock follows from the 'about 4 p. m.' decision; the OR gives no clock for the stand.

notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: CORRECTED. Farnham (OR): the regiment "ordered, alone, by General Robinson, to take possession of a hill which commanded the road, and hold the same as long as there was a man left", held until, "finding the enemy in such force" and no support, it fell back into the hollow and the woods and "ordered a retreat, but not in time to reach the main body of the brigade"; loss of the day 223 (officers killed 1, men killed 8, officers wounded 5, men wounded 47, officers missing 11, men missing 151). Maine at Gettysburg (1898): "It was about four o'clock in the afternoon when the Sixteenth Maine was ordered to advance", the order "Take the position and hold it at any cost"; "took position behind the stone wall, and broke the right wing to the right, parallel to the Mummasburg Road"; "In a short time, perhaps twenty minutes ... the enemy were upon them"; at the railroad cut Ewell's men and Hill's struck at once, "Colonel Tilden fell to Swell's share" (the OCR prints Swell for Ewell), "twelve officers and ninety-two enlisted men" were captured and "thirty-five in all, and four officers" escaped to Cemetery Hill; the marker: killed 11, wounded 62, captured 159 out of 275 engaged. Fox: of 248 engaged, 9 killed, 59 wounded, 164 captured, "2 officers and 15 men alone remained". NOT in any source read: 298 men engaged (the seed); the figures 275 and 248 differ and are both carried; the OR report gives no hour for the stand (Robinson: nearly 5 p. m. for the orders to withdraw, 4 p. m. is the Maine marker's hour); 16:30 (the seed's Wikipedia value) is not in any report. Remains unsupported: 298 men engaged (no source read has the figure; 275 and 248 are the two printed figures); an hour of the stand in any report (Farnham gives none; the hour about four o'clock is the regiment's account of 1898).

notes: Close-out 2026-11-13: CORRECTED. Hancock: "Orders were at once given to establish a line of battle on Cemetery Hill, with skirmishers occupying that part of the town immediately in our front"; Wadsworth's division and a battery (thought to be the Fifth Maine) "were placed on the eminence just across the turnpike"; Geary's division went "to the high ground to the right of and near Round Top Mountain"; he sent Meade a communication "informing him that the position at Gettysburg was a very strong one, having for its disadvantage that it might be easily turned, and leaving to him the responsibility whether the battle should be fought at Gettysburg or at a place first selected by him". His 5.25 dispatch: "We have now taken up a position in the cemetery, and cannot well be taken. It is a position, however, easily turned ... I think we can retire; if not, we can fight here". Howard: after learning of Reynolds' death (about 11.30) he "came to the conclusion that the only tenable position for my limited force was the ridge to the southeast of Gettysburg, now so well known as Cemetery Ridge" and set up headquarters near the cemetery; Wadsworth's division "was sent to occupy a height to the right and rear of our position". Meade: "the reports from Major-Generals Hancock and Howard on the character of the position being favorable, I determined to give battle at this point". Howard's evening letter: "This evening I have read an order stating that if General Slocum was present he would assume command ... The above has mortified me and will disgrace me." NOT in any text read: Doubleday's statement that Howard resisted and Hancock's marginal note denying it (neither book is in the library; Howard's own account is that they "agreed at once"); Hancock choosing Gettysburg as the battlefield (the reports have Howard choosing the ground and Meade deciding the battle). Remains unsupported: Doubleday's statement that Howard resisted and Hancock's marginal note denying it (neither text is in the library).
notes_before: Hancock selecting the ground and ordering the line is primary. Doubleday's charge that Howard resisted, Hancock's marginal note denying it and Howard's 'mortified me' are not in these OR passages (WHN secondary; Howard's later writing not read).

Ewell: "Early entering by the York Railroad at the same time that Rodes came in on the Cashtown road, they together captured over 4,000 prisoners and three pieces of artillery"; "no other troops than those of this corps entered the town at all". Rodes: his first line extended "from the left of the center of the town along one of its principal streets and out on the road to Fairfield"; the second line (Daniel and O'Neal) along the railroad. Early: "Hays' brigade was formed in line in the street running through the middle of the town". Hill: "These two divisions were bivouacked in the positions won". Perrin: the charge went on "until we got within 200 yards of their last position, about the theological college". Doubleday: he "remained at the seminary superintending the final movement" until "thousands of hostile bayonets made their appearance around the sides of the building". Jacobs (1864): "At the close of the fight, Ewell's corps occupied the town"; Rodes' division "occupying Middle street as far west as the Seminary hill"; "Hill's corps took position on the Seminary ridge"; "General Lee had reconnoitred our position from the College cupola". Bachelder (1873): "The Seminary building was directly in the line of the Confederate army after the first day's fight; and was occupied as a hospital during and after the battle" (1889: "occupied during and after the battle as a Union hospital"); the College "used as a Confederate hospital". Hospital Scenes (1864): "sharp-shooters, who were on the tops of the houses"; Tillie Pierce: sharpshooters "would enter the cellar in search of eatables"; NPS: Federal soldiers "cut off from friendly lines, hid in cellars and outbuildings". corrected_claim_text: Ewell: "Early entering by the York Railroad at the same time that Rodes came in on the Cashtown road, they together captured over 4,000 prisoners and three pieces of artillery"; "no other troops than those of this corps entered the town at all". Rodes: his first line extended "from the left of the center of the town along one of its principal streets and out on the road to Fairfield"; the second line (Daniel and O'Neal) along the railroad. Early: "Hays' brigade was formed in line in the street running through the middle of the town". Hill: "These two divisions were bivouacked in the positions won". Perrin: the charge went on "until we got within 200 yards of their last position, about the theological college". Doubleday: he "remained at the seminary superintending the final movement" until "thousands of hostile bayonets made their appearance around the sides of the building". Jacobs (1864): "At the close of the fight, Ewell's corps occupied the town"; Rodes' division "occupying Middle street as far west as the Seminary hill"; "Hill's corps took position on the Seminary ridge"; "General Lee had reconnoitred our position from the College cupola". Bachelder (1873): "The Seminary building was directly in the line of the Confederate army after the first day's fight; and was occupied as a hospital during and after the battle" (1889: "occupied during and after the battle as a Union hospital"); the College "used as a Confederate hospital". Hospital Scenes (1864): "sharp-shooters, who were on the tops of the houses"; Tillie Pierce: sharpshooters "would enter the cellar in search of eatables"; NPS: Federal soldiers "cut off from friendly lines, hid in cellars and outbuildings". The sources for the houses, the food and the cellars describe the days of the battle, not the afternoon of Jul 1 alone; no source gives an hour for the taking of the seminary building or of Pennsylvania Hall, which the 45th New York was preparing to defend about 4 p. m.; no clock offset is applied.
